# AI-Assisted Authoring {#sec-ai-authoring}

```{python}
#| include: false
import pointblank as pb
pb.config(report_incl_header=False, report_incl_footer=False)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## These examples call a language model
The features in this chapter need the generation extras, installed with
`pip install "pointblank[generate]"`, and an API key for a model provider. A book render cannot
reach a provider, so the calls below are marked `#| eval: false` and are not run. `DraftValidation`
and `EditValidation` are also marked experimental in the library, so their interfaces may change.
:::

The previous chapter used a language model to judge data. This chapter uses one to help write the
validation plan. When you are faced with an unfamiliar table with dozens of columns, the hardest part
is often getting started and deciding which checks are worth writing. Pointblank can take a first
pass at this for you. It can draft a plan from scratch, revise an existing plan based on an
instruction, or suggest what a plan is missing. In every case you review the proposal before
anything is accepted.

It helps to know up front what the model is sent. It does not get the full table. Instead, Pointblank
sends a `DataScan` profile, the same kind of summary described in @sec-inspecting-data. The profile
includes the row count, the column names and types, summary statistics for each column (such as the
number of missing values, the minimum, and the maximum), and a short sample of five values from each
column. So a small amount of real data does leave your machine, which matters if some columns are
sensitive. We use `game_revenue` for the examples.

```{python}
game_revenue = pb.load_dataset(dataset="game_revenue", tbl_type="polars")
```

The most common starting point is asking the model to draft a plan.

## Drafting a plan with `DraftValidation`

The `DraftValidation` class profiles a table and asks a model to propose a complete validation plan
for it. You create it with the data and a model name, and displaying the result shows a
`pb.Validate(...)` chain that you can copy into your code and edit.

```{python}
#| eval: false
pb.DraftValidation(data=game_revenue, model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-5")
```

The draft comes back as Python code. A typical draft checks the schema, checks the identifier
columns for nulls, limits the numeric columns to the ranges seen in the profile, and limits
columns with few distinct values to the values seen in the profile. It is a starting point, not a
finished plan. The model knows what the data looks like right now, but not what your business rules
require, so you edit the draft to match your intent, such as replacing an observed range with a real
limit or removing a check that does not matter. The generated code is available as the object's
`code` attribute, and the `validate_syntax()` method checks that it parses before you run it.

When reviewing a draft, pay the most attention to the ranges and sets. A drafted check describes
what the data currently is, not what it should be. The largest `item_revenue` in `game_revenue` is
142.99, so a draft might propose that the column stays below 150. That describes the current data,
but it will fail the first time a legitimate larger purchase comes in. Treat each drafted range as
a question: is this a real limit, or just the range the model happened to see? Where the two differ,
replace the observed number with the one you actually intend. The model cannot make this call for
you, which is why a draft is only a first pass.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A draft describes the data, not your intent
A drafted check reflects what the data happens to contain, not what your business rules require.
Check every generated range and set, and replace observed values with intended ones before
accepting it. Otherwise a check that only describes today's data will fail on tomorrow's normal
data.
:::

## Editing a plan with `EditValidation`

Once you have a plan, `EditValidation` revises it based on a plain-language instruction. This is
useful when you know what change you want but would rather describe it than edit the code by hand.
You give it the plan, an instruction, and a model, and optionally the data so the model can take the
table's actual columns and values into account. We start with a small plan written by hand.

```{python}
base = (
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue, tbl_name="game_revenue")
    .col_vals_gt(columns="session_duration", value=0)
    .col_vals_not_null(columns="player_id")
)
```

That is an ordinary `Validate` object. Asking for a change gives you a proposal, not a modified
plan, and you look at the proposal before accepting it.

```{python}
#| eval: false
edit = pb.EditValidation(
    validation=base,
    instruction="Also require item_revenue to be non-negative and item_type to be one of iap or ad.",
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-5",
    data=game_revenue,
)

print(edit.diff())
```

The `diff()` method shows the change as a text diff. The `changed_steps()` method lists the changes
as structured records of added, removed, and modified steps, and `review()` shows the change as a
table. When you are happy with it, `accept()` runs the revised code and returns a new `Validate`
object that you can interrogate.

```{python}
#| eval: false
revised = edit.accept()
revised.interrogate()
```

Nothing changes until you call `accept()`. You can also start from a plan stored as a code string,
a YAML string, or a file path instead of a `Validate` object, so `EditValidation` works just as
well with plans kept in version control as with plans in a notebook.

## Authoring from a prompt with `from_prompt`

If you have no plan yet and would rather describe the checks in words than start from a generated
draft, the `from_prompt()` method on `Validate` builds a plan from a plain-language description. It
starts from an empty plan, keeps the table name, label, and any thresholds you set, and returns an
`EditValidation`, so you review and accept the result the same way as an edit.

```{python}
#| eval: false
proposal = (
    pb.Validate(data=game_revenue, tbl_name="game_revenue")
    .from_prompt(
        prompt="Ensure player_id and session_id are never null and item_revenue is never negative.",
        model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-5",
    )
)

plan = proposal.accept()
```

The difference from `DraftValidation` is where you start. A draft starts from the data and proposes
whatever looks worth checking. The `from_prompt()` method starts from what you say you want and turns
it into steps, so it suits the case where you already know what to check and just want it written
as code.

## Suggesting improvements

The `suggest_improvements()` method starts from a plan you already have and proposes what it is
missing. It profiles the table, looks for gaps, such as columns that no step checks or steps that
could use thresholds, and returns an `EditValidation` with the proposed additions for you to review.

```{python}
#| eval: false
proposal = base.suggest_improvements(model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-5")

print(proposal.diff())
improved = proposal.accept()
```

Use this to fill out a plan that works but may not be thorough. It is easy to miss gaps when you
write checks one at a time. As with the other tools here, the additions only take effect once you
accept them.

## The interactive assistant

For exploratory work, the `assistant()` function opens a chat session about a table. You can ask
what checks make sense, ask for a plan, or refine one over several messages rather than with a
single instruction.

```{python}
#| eval: false
pb.assistant(model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-5", data=game_revenue, tbl_name="game_revenue")
```

The assistant is most useful when you are first getting to know a dataset and are still working out
what to check. It works alongside the exploration tools of @sec-inspecting-data.

## Choosing and combining the tools

Which tool to use depends on where you are starting. If you have an unfamiliar table and no plan,
`DraftValidation` is the fastest way to get a draft, and `assistant()` suits the same situation if
you would rather work through it in a conversation. If you know what you want to check but have no
plan yet, `from_prompt()` turns your description into steps. If you already have a plan and want a
specific change, `EditValidation` makes it from an instruction. And if you want to know what a
working plan is missing, `suggest_improvements()` proposes additions.

The tools also work well in sequence. For example, you might draft a plan with `DraftValidation`,
refine it with one or two `EditValidation` instructions, fill gaps with `suggest_improvements()`,
and, after reviewing and accepting each proposal, export the finished plan with `to_yaml()` so it can
be kept in version control (see @sec-yaml-workflows). Since the edit tools accept a YAML string or
file path, you can pick that stored plan up and revise it later the same way. The model speeds up
each step, but the plan that ends up in the repository is one a person reviewed and accepted. Keep in
mind that `DraftValidation` and `EditValidation` are experimental, and model output is not
deterministic, so two drafts of the same table can differ. That is one more reason to review
everything.

## What the model sees, and what it cannot write back

There are two limits to keep in mind across all of these features. The first is what the model is
sent. It gets the `DataScan` profile described at the start of this chapter: summary statistics plus
a five-value sample from each column. The rest of the table stays on your machine, but those sample
values do not. If a column holds personal or confidential information, its sample values will be
included in the request. For sensitive data, consider a local model through `"ollama"`, or write the
plan by hand.

The second limit comes from how the edit tools work, which is by converting the plan to `to_code()`
text and back. As described in @sec-advanced-validation, that text form cannot represent everything.
When a plan goes through the AI tools, the expressions in `col_vals_expr()`, `conjointly()`, and
`specially()` become placeholders, `pre=` functions and step `actions=` are dropped, a callable
`active=` becomes `True`, and `col_vals_in_table()` steps are left out. Pointblank warns you when
this happens. Plans built from the other built-in checks come through unchanged, but plans that rely
on custom Python logic need that logic added back by hand after an edit.
